prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

      "No dedicated cycling facilities, transit stops, or other clearly visible low-carbon mobility features are present in the scene."
    ],

      "The street appears clean and orderly, with well-maintained paving, façades, and little visible litter or clutter.",
      "The buildings have a fairly consistent residential scale and subdued color palette, creating visual coherence along the corridor.",
      "Aesthetic quality is reduced somewhat by blank garage-like ground floors, parked cars, and extensive paved surfaces that make the street feel somewhat plain."
    ],

      "Physical comfort is supported by smooth pavement surfaces and relatively even walking areas along both sides of the street.",
      "Thermal comfort is only moderate because tree cover is sparse and much of the street and sidewalk area is exposed to direct sun.",
      "Psychological comfort benefits from the quiet residential setting and low apparent traffic, but the lack of seating, shade structures, and richer street activity limits overall comfort."
    ],
    "walkability": [
      "Walkability is helped by the presence of continuous paved pedestrian margins on both sides of the street and a calm residential context.",
      "It is weakened by the lack of clearly marked sidewalks separated from driveways and parking access, especially on the right where vehicles occupy edge space.",
      "No visible crosswalks, pedestrian priority markings, or wayfinding elements are present, so walking routes appear functional but not strongly prioritized."
    ]

justice: Both sides of the street appear to provide pedestrian space, with paved edge zones beside the carriageway rather than forcing all users into the vehicle lane.
Accessibility is only moderate because no marked curb ramps, tactile paving, or designated crossing points are visible at the edges of the roadway.

Spatial allocation still favors vehicle access and parking, shown by the wide central asphalt lane and parked cars along the right side, which reduces the sense of equal priority for non-motorized users.
safety: The street appears to have low traffic volume, with only a few parked vehicles and a relatively narrow residential roadway, which likely lowers conflict risk.
Safety is weakened by the absence of visible lane markings, speed-control devices, zebra crossings, or traffic calming elements that would clearly organize movement.
Building fronts, windows, and entrances face the street on both sides, providing some natural surveillance and improving perceived personal safety.
livability: The street has a residential character with multiple building entrances, balconies, and small frontage spaces, supporting everyday neighborhood use.
Trees and planted pots on the left side add some human-scale greenery and make the environment feel more habitable than a fully paved lane.
Livability is limited by the lack of visible public amenities such as benches, play areas, shops, or community gathering features along the street.
sustainability: Some street trees and small planted areas are present on the left side, offering limited ecological and microclimate benefits.
Most of the visible ground surface is hard paving or asphalt, with little permeable landscape area or stormwater infrastructure evident.
No dedicated cycling facilities, transit stops, or other clearly visible low-carbon mobility features are present in the scene.
aesthetics: The street appears clean and orderly, with well-maintained paving, façades, and little visible litter or clutter.
The buildings have a fairly consistent residential scale and subdued color palette, creating visual coherence along the corridor.
Aesthetic quality is reduced somewhat by blank garage-like ground floors, parked cars, and extensive paved surfaces that make the street feel somewhat plain.
comfort: Physical comfort is supported by smooth pavement surfaces and relatively even walking areas along both sides of the street.
Thermal comfort is only moderate because tree cover is sparse and much of the street and sidewalk area is exposed to direct sun.
Psychological comfort benefits from the quiet residential setting and low apparent traffic, but the lack of seating, shade structures, and richer street activity limits overall comfort.
walkability: Walkability is helped by the presence of continuous paved pedestrian margins on both sides of the street and a calm residential context.
It is weakened by the lack of clearly marked sidewalks separated from driveways and parking access, especially on the right where vehicles occupy edge space.
No visible crosswalks, pedestrian priority markings, or wayfinding elements are present, so walking routes appear functional but not strongly prioritized.

prompt_c3:
As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

"Separated bike lanes reduce conflict with vehicles",

"Clear separation between sidewalk and driveway enhances walking safety"
],

"Proximity to convenience stores and community facilities meets daily needs",
"Pedestrian activity on the street increases community vitality"
],

1. All scores must include one decimal place.
2. Each array in explanations must contain at least 3 reasons based on specific objects in the image (e.g., benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings).
3. Analysis content must strictly match the persona setting; generic evaluations unrelated to the specified perspective are strictly prohibited.
4. Do not mention RAG, retrieval, or prompt instructions in the explanations.

Environmental quality and aesthetics (i) Vegetation and water: Every study reported that attractive greenery—street trees, front gardens, or small parks—pulled walkers onto a route. The only counter-example was the Dutch “green strips” noted by Borst et al. (2009), which participants saw as unsafe because they limited visibility. Water features (ponds, fountains, seafronts) and, in one study, the chance of meeting animals further boosted route appeal (Van Cauwenberg et al., 2012). (ii) Cleanliness, noise, and air: Litter-free streets and well-maintained façades were repeatedly linked to comfort, whereas noise and exhaust fumes discouraged walking (Moran et al., 2017; Van Cauwenberg et al., 2012). (iii) Traffic volume: Findings on traffic counts were mixed: heavy flows were associated with danger, yet Borst et al. (2009)observed the opposite in some Dutch streets, suggesting that clear, predictable vehicle streams can make a route easier to navigate. 6 N. Fulman et al. Blind walls (without windows) and tight enclosures reduced use (Borst et al., 2009); routes offering long sight-lines or low-rise skylines fostered feelings of safety and relaxation (Van Cauwenberg et al., 2012). 3.5.3. Access to facilities and other environmental attributes (i) Everyday amenities: Routes that passed caf´es, food shops, banks, or health services were consistently favored, largely because they enabled multipurpose trips (e.g., exercise plus errands). (ii) Rest opportunities and transit links: Benches, shade, and other rest areas let participants extend their walking range, while nearby public-transport stops helped them combine walking with longer journeys (Moran et al., 2017; Van Cauwenberg et al., 2012). (iii) Perceived personal safety: Fear of unfamiliar people, poor surveillance, or “street disorder” diminished route attractiveness in four studies (Van Cauwenberg et al., 2012; Mitra et al., 2015; Brookfield and Tilley, 2016; Buman et al., 2013). 3.5.4. Individual and neighborhood factors (i) Neighborhood context: Only three studies linked route choice to neighborhood characteristics. Moran et al. (2017)saw few socioeconomic-related differences apart from affluent residents citing better sidewalks and logging longer walks. On the other hand, Buman et al. (2013) and Mitra et al. (2015) showed that concerns varied by housing type: suburban or low-income complexes emphasized sidewalk condition and personal safety more than dense, downtown condominium areas.
